questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What sets the risk window when a fix is passed along a chain
questions.learningObjective: Identify what sets the risk window in a multi-step fix chain
questions.stem: Survey form 4 records a fix moving from a field station to a regional office to a funder; which factor sets the risk window in that chain?

options.text: The number of people who read the report, because each reader can act on the fix
options.misconception: confuses communication volume with repair speed

options.text: The size of the installed base at the station, because more devices mean more exposure
options.misconception: measures exposure by device count rather than delay

options.text: The time each approving step takes, because the risk window is set by the slowest link
The age of the equipment at the station, because older hardware patches more slowly
options.misconception: blames the hardware for an approval delay

questions.explanation: The risk window in a fix chain is set by the slowest approving step, since the flaw stays live until the last approval lands. Device counts and reader numbers describe exposure, not delay.
questions.hint: The window is the slowest link.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a bounty programme lists what it excludes
questions.learningObjective: Explain what an exclusion list achieves for a bounty programme
questions.stem: The survey asks why a programme's published terms list categories that are out of scope; explain what the exclusion list achieves.

answer.exemplar: The exclusion list does two things at once. It defines the boundary of what the programme will pay for, so reporters and triagers apply the same test and effort goes into finding accepted flaws rather than disputing scope. It also reduces the legal and safety risk of the programme itself, because methods that cannot be tested in a controlled way, such as physical intrusion or attacks on staff, are removed from scope rather than argued about case by case. Without the list, every report becomes a scope negotiation.

questions.explanation: The list fixes a shared boundary for what counts and removes methods the programme will not run, keeping triagers consistent and the programme safe. Without it every report becomes an argument about scope.
questions.hint: Scope is decided once, in advance.

options.misconception: treats encryption and long life as protective

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What sets the risk window when a fix is passed along a chain
questions.learningObjective: Explain what determines the length of a risk window
questions.stem: The survey asks what decides how long a known flaw stays live in a multi-step fix chain; explain the factors the survey identifies.

answer.exemplar: The survey identifies three factors. The first is the slowest approval step, since the chain cannot finish faster than its slowest gate. The second is the time each approver needs to believe the problem is real, which depends on how well the report is evidenced rather than on technical difficulty. The third is the size of the deployment step itself, because a fix that needs a site visit or a device replacement carries a very different window from one that can be pushed by configuration change.

questions.explanation: The window is set by the slowest gate, by how convincingly the report is evidenced, and by how the fix must be deployed. Treating it as pure technical difficulty misses the approval steps.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The verification that stops an active interception
questions.learningObjective: Explain why encryption alone cannot stop an interception
questions.stem: The survey asks why an encrypted but unsigned telemetry link can still be tampered with in the field; explain what verification adds.

answer.exemplar: Encryption protects a message from anyone who cannot read the key, but on a station link the attacker sits at the relay, where the connection is established. A relay in that position can terminate the connection and present itself as the far end, so the ciphertext it delivers is perfectly well formed. Signing changes the picture because the receiver checks a signature against a key it already trusts, not against something the relay supplied. A modified payload then fails that check, so the alteration is detected rather than merely hidden.

questions.explanation: Encryption alone lets a party who can terminate the connection substitute a well-formed message; a signature checked against a pre-trusted key exposes the change. Transport security does not establish the sender.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What stops credential stuffing
questions.learningObjective: Explain why password rules do not stop a stuffing run
questions.stem: The survey asks why blocking obvious password reuse still leaves stations exposed to credential stuffing; explain the gap.

answer.exemplar: The gap is that a password blocklist only removes the weakest reused pairs, while a stuffing run tries billions of combinations, most of them valid on someone. A station with 400 accounts can absorb hundreds of thousands of guesses, and a blocklist of a few thousand common passwords removes only the head of that distribution. What actually cuts the run is a control that limits attempts rather than a control that judges password quality, because the run's success does not depend on the password being weak.

questions.explanation: A blocklist removes only the weakest pairs while a stuffing run tries vast numbers of plausible ones. The run depends on attempt volume, which password quality rules do not constrain.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The verification that stops an active interception
questions.learningObjective: Select verification that detects a terminating relay

stimulus.body: A survey sheet records that station telemetry travels over a link where the relay terminates the connection to the vendor. Packets are encrypted end to end, but each batch carries only a CRC checksum.

questions.stem: The survey sheet describes an encrypted link with a checksum only; which verification would detect interception here?

options.text: A longer encryption key, so the relay cannot decrypt and re-encrypt the batch
options.misconception: assumes key length defeats a terminating relay

options.text: A digital signature the receiver checks against the station's registered key
A checksum that includes a secret value, so the relay cannot recompute it
options.misconception: calls a keyed checksum a signature without checking identity

options.text: A challenge sent to the relay, so the relay proves it is not in the path
options.misconception: invents a relay challenge that would not change the result

questions.explanation: A relay that terminates the connection can produce a well-formed encrypted batch, so the receiver needs a check tied to the station's identity rather than to the data alone. A signature against a registered key gives exactly that.
questions.hint: Tie the check to the station's key.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a bounty programme lists what it excludes
questions.learningObjective: Specify how an exclusion list should be drafted
questions.stem: The survey asks how a programme should phrase its exclusion list so that reporters and triagers work from the same standard; explain the drafting requirements.

answer.exemplar: The list has to be written so that two independent people reach the same answer. That means naming the boundary in terms of what can be tested, not in terms of abstract categories such as interesting findings or severe issues. It means stating where the line sits for the cases most likely to be argued about, such as third-party services and physical testing, because those are where the ambiguity actually lives. It also means saying what happens to a report that turns out to sit outside, so reporters know the outcome and triagers know the procedure.

questions.explanation: A useful scope is written in testable terms, settles the cases most likely to be disputed, and states what happens to out-of-scope reports. Vague wording leaves two people applying different rules.
questions.hint: Write the rule, not the category.

options.misconception: invents a labelling error as the main risk

questions.explanation: Without a check tied to the station's identity, a party who can terminate the connection can claim to be the station and deliver altered readings. Expiry and retries are separate issues.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What sets the risk window when a fix is passed along a chain
questions.learningObjective: Identify levers that shorten a risk window without engineering
questions.stem: The survey asks which levers a station manager can pull to shorten the risk window without speeding up technical work; explain the levers the survey names.

answer.exemplar: The survey names three levers that sit outside engineering. First, the report itself: a finding that reproduces in one step, on the vendor's own hardware, with a clear impact statement moves through an approval chain much faster than one that needs the reviewer to reconstruct the problem. Second, the chain's shape: naming one accountable owner at each step, with a deadline attached, removes the waiting that comes from routing decisions. Third, the deployment plan: a fix that can be applied remotely shortens the window between the vendor releasing it and the station running it.

questions.explanation: The survey points to evidence quality, accountable ownership with deadlines and deployment method, none of which need faster coding. Assuming only engineering effort matters misses where the waiting happens.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The verification that stops an active interception
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a name check is not identity proof
questions.stem: The survey asks why a certificate check by name alone was not enough at the station relay; explain what the relay can do and what closes the gap.

answer.exemplar: Checking the certificate's name proves that the far end holds a certificate for that host, but it does not prove that the far end is the station. A relay that sits between the two ends can present its own valid certificate for that same name, especially where the station and the vendor share a naming authority, and the receiving side has no way to distinguish it from the genuine article. The gap closes when the receiver checks something the relay cannot obtain, such as a signature made with the station's registered key or a pinned value that was agreed out of band.

questions.explanation: A name check proves who the far end claims to be, not who it is, so a relay holding a valid certificate for that name can impersonate the station. Only a check tied to something the relay lacks closes the gap.
questions.hint: Names can be copied; keys cannot.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What stops credential stuffing
questions.learningObjective: Explain why unique passwords do not stop a stuffing run
questions.stem: The survey asks why telling users to use unique passwords for every service does not stop credential stuffing at a station; explain the gap.

answer.exemplar: Unique passwords break the link between services, which stops a breach at one site becoming a breach elsewhere. They do not stop the run itself, because a stuffing list is built from breached credentials and email addresses, not from the target's own password policy. If a station account appears in that list with a password the user never changed, the guess is already correct and no password hygiene on the station's side affects it. The run continues regardless of what the station tells its users to do, so the controls that matter are the ones applied to attempts rather than to passwords.

questions.explanation: Unique passwords protect other services, but a stuffing list already carries credentials and identifiers, so correct guesses happen regardless of station policy. Controls that cap attempts stop the run.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a bounty programme lists what it excludes
questions.learningObjective: Explain the credibility risk of a changing scope
questions.stem: The survey asks what happens to a programme's credibility when its exclusion list changes over time; explain the risk the survey identifies.

answer.exemplar: The risk is that scope becomes a moving target. If an exclusion list is revised case by case, reporters who already spent effort on a class of testing learn afterwards that it did not count, and word spreads that the programme pays only for the findings it already wanted. The other damage is internal: triagers applying a revised scope inconsistently start rejecting reports that an earlier version of the terms would have paid, which makes each decision look arbitrary. Publishing revisions with reasons, and keeping earlier versions available, lets a programme change without making its own standard unpredictable.

questions.explanation: Changing scope case by case punishes reporters who invested effort and makes triagers look arbitrary, so credibility suffers. Publishing reasoned revisions with old versions kept preserves predictability.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What sets the risk window when a fix is passed along a chain
questions.learningObjective: Specify what a risk window report must state
questions.stem: The survey asks a station manager to describe the risk window when reporting it upward; explain what the description must contain.

answer.exemplar: The description has to name four things or it cannot be used to prioritise. When the flaw became known at the station, which fixes the start of the window and stops the report being read as a general worry. What the flaw allows in the meantime, since that sets how much attention the window deserves. The earliest date a fix could realistically be running, which depends on the chain rather than on hope. And the date the window would close if the chain stalls, which is what makes the ask specific.

questions.explanation: A useful risk statement names the window's start, the impact during it, the earliest realistic fix date and the closing date if the chain stalls. Without those four the report cannot be prioritised.
